conquered the Near East region. The Ayyubids ruled much of the Middle East during the 12th and 13th centuries,
controlling Egypt, Syria, northern Mesopotamia, Hejaz, Yemen, and the North African coast up to the borders of
modern-day Tunisia. After Saladin, his sons contested control over the sultanate, but Saladin's brother al-Adil
eventually established himself in 1200. In the 1230s, Syria's Ayyubid rulers attempted to win independence from Egypt
and remained divided until Egyptian Sultan as-Salih Ayyub restored Ayyubid unity by taking over most of Syria,
excluding <color=#3366CC>Aleppo</color>, by 1247. In 1250, the dynasty in the Egyptian region was overthrown by slave regiments. A number
of attempts to recover it failed, led by an-Nasir Yusuf of Aleppo. In 1260, the Mongols sacked Aleppo and wrested
control of what remained of the Ayyubid territories soon after.

Turco-Mongol conversion
Mongol period
While the Abbasid Caliphate suffered a decline following the reign of al-Wathiq (842–847) and <color=#3366CC>al-Mu'tadid</color> (892–902),
the <color=#3366CC>Mongol Empire</color> put an end to the Abbasid dynasty in 1258. The <color=#3366CC>Mongols</color> spread throughout <color=#3366CC>Central Asia</color> and
<color=#3366CC>Persia</color>; the Persian city of <color=#3366CC>Isfahan</color> had fallen to them by 1237.
The Ilkhans of Chingisid descendence understood themselves as defenders of Islam, perhaps even as the legitimate
heirs of the Abbasid Caliphate. Al-Nuwayri, stated that the Mongols had heavenly approval and would live in
accordance with the restrictions of <color=#3366CC>Islamic law</color>. Some <color=#3366CC>Sufi Muslim</color> writers, such as the Persian poet and mystic <color=#3366CC>Jalāl</color>
<color=#3366CC>ad-Dīn Muhammad Rūmī</color> and his biographer Šams al-Dīn Ahmad Aflākī, regarded the Mongols and <color=#3366CC>Turkic peoples</color>
from the <color=#3366CC>Eurasian Steppe</color> as more pious than the <color=#3366CC>Muslim scholars</color>, <color=#3366CC>ascetics</color>, and muftis of their time, and hence
expressed favor of their conquests, considering the <color=#3366CC>invasion</color> as divine punishment from God. Aflaki identifies the
invasion with a hadith, describing the Turks (and Mongols) as the army of Muhammad's wrath. In his Manaqib al-'Arifin,
the Turks and Mongols are described as God's "punishment from hell", and by that, people who follow the will of the
Creator.
Many scholars had argued that the conversion of the Turks and Mongols has been filtered through the mediation of
<color=#3366CC>Persian</color> and <color=#3366CC>Central Asian</color> culture. Rather than converting to Islamic orthodoxy, they encountered Islam mostly through
the preaching of <color=#3366CC>Sufi Muslim</color> wandering ascetics and mystics (fakirs and dervishes). Recently this view has been
challenged on grounds that a defined Islamic orthodoxy has not yet existed during the conversion of the Turks and
Mongols.
In the 13th to the 14th centuries, both <color=#3366CC>Sunnī</color> and <color=#3366CC>Shīa</color> practices were intertwined, and historical figures commonly
associated with the history of Shīa Islam, like <color=#3366CC>Alī ibn Abī Tālib</color> and <color=#3366CC>Jafar al-Sādiq</color> (respectively, the first and sixth <color=#3366CC>Shīīte</color>
<color=#3366CC>Imams</color>), played an almost universal role for Muslim believers to understand "the Unseen" (al-Ghaib). A sharp distinction
between Sunnī, Shīa, and heterodox Islamic beliefs did not exist. Therefore, ideas from foreign cultures were easier to
integrate into the Islamic worldview. During this era, the Persian Sufi poet and mystic <color=#3366CC>Jalaluddin Rumi</color> (1207–1273)
wrote his masterpiece, the <color=#3366CC>Masnavi</color>, which he believed to be "sent down" from God and understood it as the <color=#3366CC>proper</color>
<color=#3366CC>explanation of the Quran</color> (tafsīr). According to Aflaki, the invading Mongols were impressed by Rumi's devotion to God,
so they did not assault him, believing it would cause the wrath of God upon them.
On the other hand, Turks and Mongols also faced criticism. Opposition to them have been formulated by <color=#3366CC>Ibn Taymiyya</color>
(1263–1328), who did not accept the Mongols' conversion to Sunnism. Feeling threatened by the <color=#3366CC>Crusaders</color> and the
<color=#3366CC>Mongols</color>, ibn Taymiyya called for elimination by <color=#3366CC>a militant jihād</color> against whom he deemed "heretic", including <color=#3366CC>Shias</color>,
<color=#3366CC>al-Ashariyya</color> and <color=#3366CC>falāsifa</color> (philosophers), and established his own theological doctrines. His theology was characterized
by a literal understanding of the Quran, a <color=#3366CC>physicalist ontology</color>, and a rejection of most philosophical and mystical
approaches in favor of a simplistic and dogmatic theology.
Another unique characteristic of his theological approach was the importance of a <color=#3366CC>theocratic state</color>. Prior to ibn
Taimiyya, religious wisdom was meant to guide governmental authorities, while ibn Taymiyya demanded <color=#3366CC>political power</color>
to promote religious piety. Having a deep-rooting discern for the Mongols, ibn Taimiyya sought to pronounce takfīr
(excommunication) upon the Turco-Mongol rulers, despite their profession of the <color=#3366CC>shahada</color> (Islamic testimony of faith),
or regular observance of <color=#3366CC>as-Salāh</color> (obligatory prayers), <color=#3366CC>sawm</color> (fasting) and other expressions of religiosity. His disciple
<color=#3366CC>ibn Kathir</color> ( d. 1373), propounded the same belief in his tafsīr.
During his lifetime, ibn Taimiyya played only a marginal role and most of his writings were rejected. He was repeatedly
accused of blasphemy by anthropomorphizing God, and his disciple <color=#3366CC>Ibn Kathir</color> distanced himself from his mentor. Yet,
some of Ibn Taymiyya's teaching influenced Ibn Kathir's methodology on tafsīr, discounted much of the exegetical
tradition since then. Only centuries later, among <color=#3366CC>Wahhabis</color> and in 21st century <color=#3366CC>Salafism</color>, their writings gained notable
importance.
Islamic Mongol empires
Ultimately, the <color=#3366CC>Ilkhanate</color>, <color=#3366CC>Golden Horde</color>, and the <color=#3366CC>Chagatai Khanate</color> – three of the four principal Mongol khanates –
embraced Islam. In power in Syria, Mesopotamia, Persia, and further east, over the rest of the 13th century gradually
all converted to Islam. Most Ilkhanid rulers were replaced by the new Mongol power founded by <color=#3366CC>Timur</color> (himself a
Muslim), who conquered Persia in the 1360s, and moved against the <color=#3366CC>Delhi Sultanate</color> in India and the Ottoman Turks in
<color=#3366CC>Anatolia</color>. Timur's ceaseless conquests were accompanied by displays of brutality matched only by <color=#3366CC>Chinggis Khan</color>,
whose example Timur consciously imitated. <color=#3366CC>Samarqand</color>, the cosmopolitan capital of Timur's empire, flourished under
his rule as never before, while Iran and Iraq suffered large-scale devastation. Muslim scholars, such as <color=#3366CC>Nasir al-Din</color>
<color=#3366CC>al-Tusi</color> and Qutb al-Din al-Shirazi, studied in the Maragheh observatory, erected by <color=#3366CC>Hulegu Khan</color>.
The Middle East was still recovering from the <color=#3366CC>Black Death</color>, which may have killed one third of the population in the
region. The plague began in China, and reached <color=#3366CC>Alexandria</color> in Egypt in 1347, spreading over the following years to
most Islamic areas. The combination of the plague and the wars left the Middle Eastern Islamic world in a seriously
weakened position. The Timurid dynasty would found many strong empires of Islam, including the <color=#3366CC>Mughals</color> of India.
Timurid Renaissance
The <color=#3366CC>Timurid Empire</color> based in <color=#3366CC>Central Asia</color> ruled by the Timurid dynasty saw a tremendous increase in the fields of <color=#3366CC>arts</color>
and <color=#3366CC>sciences</color>, spreading across both the eastern and western world.
Remarkable was the invention of Tamerlane Chess, reconstruction of the city of <color=#3366CC>Samarkand</color>, and substantial
contributions made by the family of Sultan Shah Rukh, which includes Gawhar Shad, polymath <color=#3366CC>Ulugh Begh</color>, and Sultan
Husayn Bayqara in the fields of astronomy, mathematics, and architecture. The empire received widespread support
from multiple <color=#3366CC>Islamic scholars</color> and scientists. A number of Islamic learning centres and mosques were built, most
notably the Ulugh Beg Observatory.
The prosperity of the city of <color=#3366CC>Herat</color> is said to have competed with those of <color=#3366CC>Florence</color>, the birthplace of the <color=#3366CC>Italian</color>
<color=#3366CC>Renaissance</color> as the center of a cultural rebirth.
The aspects of the Timurid Renaissance were later brought in <color=#3366CC>Mughal India</color> by the Mughal Emperors and served as a
heritage of states of the other remaining Islamic Gunpowder empires: the <color=#3366CC>Ottoman Turkey</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Safavid Iran</color>.
Mamluk Sultanate
In 1250, the Ayyubid Egyptian dynasty was overthrown by <color=#3366CC>slave regiments</color>, and the <color=#3366CC>Mamluk Sultanate</color> was born.
Military prestige was at the center of Mamluk society, and it played a key role in the confrontations with the <color=#3366CC>Mongol</color>
<color=#3366CC>Empire</color> during the <color=#3366CC>Mongol invasions of the Levant</color>.
In the 1260s, the Mongols sacked and controlled the Islamic Near East territories. The Mongol invaders were finally
stopped by Egyptian Mamluks north of Jerusalem in 1260 at the pivotal <color=#3366CC>Battle of Ain Jalut</color>. The Mamluks, who were
<color=#3366CC>slave-soldiers</color> predominantly of <color=#3366CC>Turkic</color>, Caucasian, and Southeastern European origins (see Saqaliba), forced out the
Mongols (see <color=#3366CC>Battle of Ain Jalut</color>) after the final destruction of the Ayyubid dynasty. The Mongols were again defeated
by the Mamluks at the Battle of Hims a few months later, and then driven out of Syria altogether. With this, the
Mamluks were able to concentrate their forces and to conquer the last of the <color=#3366CC>Crusader states</color> in the Levant. Thus they
united Syria and Egypt for the longest interval between the Abbasid and Ottoman empires (1250–1517).
The Mamluks experienced a continual state of political conflict, military tension, proxy wars, and economic competition
between the "Muslim territory" (Dar al-Islam) and "non-Muslim territory" (Dar al-Harb). The <color=#3366CC>Battle of Ain Jalut</color> and the
glorious Battle of Marj al-Saffar (1303), the latter partly led by Imam <color=#3366CC>Ibn Taymiyyah</color>, marked the end of the <color=#3366CC>Mongol</color>
<color=#3366CC>invasions of the Levant</color>. <color=#3366CC>Fatwas</color> given during these conflicts changed the course of Political Islam. As part of their
chosen role as defenders of Islamic orthodoxy, the Mamluks sponsored many religious buildings, including mosques,
<color=#3366CC>madrasas</color> and khanqahs. Though some construction took place in the provinces, the vast bulk of these projects
expanded the capital. Many Mamluk buildings in Cairo have survived to this day, particularly in Old Cairo (for further
informations, see Mamluk architecture).

Al-Andalus
The Arabs, under the command of the Berber General <color=#3366CC>Tarik ibn Ziyad</color>, first began their conquest of southern Spain or
al-Andalus in 711. A raiding party led by Tarik was sent to intervene in a civil war in the <color=#3366CC>Visigothic kingdom</color> in Hispania.
Crossing the <color=#3366CC>Strait of Gibraltar</color> (named after the General), it won a decisive victory in the summer of 711 when the
Visigothic king Roderic was defeated and killed on 19 July at the Battle of Guadalete. Tariq's commander, <color=#3366CC>Musa bin</color>
<color=#3366CC>Nusair</color> crossed with substantial reinforcements, and by 718 the Muslims dominated most of the peninsula. Some later
Arabic and Christian sources present an earlier raid by a certain Tārif in 710 and also, the Ad Sebastianum recension
of the Chronicle of Alfonso III, refers to an Arab attack incited by Erwig during the reign of Wamba (672–80). The two
large armies may have been in the south for a year before the decisive battle was fought.

The rulers of Al-Andalus were granted the rank of <color=#3366CC>Emir</color> by the <color=#3366CC>Umayyad</color> <color=#3366CC>Caliph</color> Al-Walid I in <color=#3366CC>Damascus</color>. After the
<color=#3366CC>Abbasids</color> came to power, some Umayyads fled to Muslim Spain to establish themselves there. By the end of the 10th
century, the ruler <color=#3366CC>Abd al-Rahman III</color> took over the title of <color=#3366CC>Caliph of Córdoba</color> (912–961). Soon after, the Umayyads went
on developing a strengthened state with its capital as <color=#3366CC>Córdoba</color>. Al-Hakam II succeeded to the Caliphate after the death
of his father Abd ar-Rahman III in 961. He secured peace with the Christian kingdoms of northern Iberia, and made use
of the stability to develop agriculture through the construction of irrigation works. Economic development was also
encouraged through the widening of streets and the building of markets. The rule of the Caliphate is known as the
heyday of Muslim presence in the peninsula.
The Umayyad Caliphate collapsed in 1031 due to political divisions and civil unrest during the rule of Hicham II who
was ousted because of his indolence. Al-Andalus then broke up into a number of states called <color=#3366CC>taifa kingdoms</color> (Arabic,
Muluk al-tawā'if; English, Petty kingdoms). The decomposition of the Caliphate into those petty kingdoms weakened the
Muslims in the Iberian Peninsula vis-à-vis the Christian kingdoms of the north. Some of the taifas, such as that of
Seville, were forced to enter into alliances with Christian princes and pay tributes in money to Castille.
Emirs of Al-Andalus
<color=#3366CC>Abd al-Rahman I</color> and Bedr (a former Greek slave) escaped with their lives after the popular revolt known as the
<color=#3366CC>Abbasid Revolution</color>. Rahman I continued south through Palestine, the Sinai, and then into Egypt. Rahman I was one of
several surviving Umayyad family members to make a perilous trek to Ifriqiya at this time. Rahman I and Bedr reached
modern day Morocco near <color=#3366CC>Ceuta</color>. Next step would be to cross to sea to al-Andalus, where Rahman I could not have
been sure whether he would be welcome. Following the Berber Revolt (740s), the province was in a state of confusion,
with the <color=#3366CC>Ummah</color> torn by tribal dissensions among the Arabs and racial tensions between the Arabs and Berbers. Bedr
lined up three Syrian commanders – Obeid Allah ibn Uthman and Abd Allah ibn Khalid, both originally of Damascus,
and Yusuf ibn Bukht of Qinnasrin and contacted al-Sumayl (then in <color=#3366CC>Zaragoza</color>) to get his consent, but al-Sumayl
refused, fearing Rahman I would try to make himself emir. After discussion with Yemenite commanders, Rahman I was
told to go to al-Andalus. Shortly thereafter, he set off with Bedr and a small group of followers for Europe. Abd
al-Rahman landed at Almuñécar in al-Andalus, to the east of <color=#3366CC>Málaga</color>.
During his brief time in Málaga, he quickly amassed local support. News of the prince's arrival spread throughout the
peninsula. In order to help speed his ascension to power, he took advantage of the feuds and dissensions. However,
before anything could be done, trouble broke out in northern al-Andalus. Abd al-Rahman and his followers were able to
<color=#3366CC>control Zaragoza</color>. Rahman I fought to rule al-Andalus in a battle at the Guadalquivir river, just outside Córdoba on the
plains of Musarah (Battle of Musarah). Rahman I was victorious, chasing his enemies from the field with parts of their
army. Rahman I marched into the capital, Córdoba, fighting off a <color=#3366CC>counterattack</color>, but negotiations ended the
confrontation. After Rahman I consolidated power, he proclaimed himself the al-Andalus emir. Rahman I did not claim
the Muslim caliph, though. The last step was to have al-Fihri's general, al-Sumayl, garroted in Córdoba's jail.
Al-Andalus was a for the house of Umayya that managed to evade the Abbasids.
In Baghdad, the Abbasid caliph <color=#3366CC>al-Mansur</color> had planned to depose the emir. Rahman I and his army confronted the
Abbasids, killing most of the Abbasid army. The main Abbasid leaders were decapitated, their heads preserved in salt,
with identifying tags pinned to their ears. The heads were bundled in a gruesome package and sent to the Abbasid
caliph who was on pilgrimage at Mecca. Rahman I quelled repeated rebellions in al-Andalus. He began the building of
the great mosque [cordova], and formed ship-yards along the coast; he is moreover said to have been the first to
transplant the palm and the pomegranate into the congenial climate of Spain: and he encouraged science and literature
in his states. He died on 29 September 788, after a reign of thirty-four years and one month.
Rahman I's successor was his son Hisham I. Born in Córdoba, he built many <color=#3366CC>mosques</color> and completed the <color=#3366CC>Mezquita</color>.
He called for a <color=#3366CC>jihad</color> that resulted in a campaign against the <color=#3366CC>Kingdom of Asturias</color> and the County of Toulouse; in this
second campaign he was defeated at Orange by William of Gellone, first cousin to <color=#3366CC>Charlemagne</color>. His successor
Al-Hakam I came to power and was challenged by his uncles, other sons of Rahman I. One, Abdallah, went to the court
of Charlemagne in <color=#3366CC>Aix-la-Chapelle</color> to negotiate for aid. In the meantime Córdoba was attacked, but was defended.
Hakam I spent much of his reign suppressing rebellions in Toledo, Saragossa and Mérida.
Abd ar-Rahman II succeeded his father and engaged in nearly continuous warfare against <color=#3366CC>Alfonso II of Asturias</color>, whose
southward advance he halted. Rahman II repulsed an assault by <color=#3366CC>Vikings</color> who had disembarked in <color=#3366CC>Cádiz</color>, conquered
<color=#3366CC>Seville</color> (with the exception of its citadel) and attacked Córdoba. Thereafter he constructed a fleet and naval arsenal at
<color=#3366CC>Seville</color> to repel future raids. He responded to William of Septimania's requests of assistance in his struggle against
<color=#3366CC>Charles the Bald</color>'s nominations.
Muhammad I's reign was marked by the movements of the Muwallad (ethnic Iberian Muslims) and Mozarabs
(Muslim-Iberia Christians). Muhammad I was succeeded by his son Mundhir I. During the reign of his father, Mundhir I
commanded military operations against the neighbouring Christian kingdoms and the Muwallad rebellions. At his
father's death, he inherited the throne. During his two-year reign, Mundhir I fought against Umar ibn Hafsun. He died in
888 at Bobastro, succeeded by his brother Abdullah ibn Muhammad al-Umawi.
Umawi showed no reluctance to dispose of those he viewed as a threat. His government was marked by continuous
wars between Arabs, Berbers and Muwallad. His power as emir was confined to the area of Córdoba, while the rest
had been seized by rebel families. The son he had designated as successor was killed by one of Umawi's brothers.
The latter was in turn executed by Umawi's father, who named as successor <color=#3366CC>Abd ar-Rahman III</color>, son of the killed son of
Umawi.

Africa
The <color=#3366CC>Umayyad conquest of North Africa</color> continued the century of rapid Muslim military expansion following the death of
<color=#3366CC>Muhammad</color> in 632. By 640 the Arabs controlled <color=#3366CC>Mesopotamia</color>, had invaded <color=#3366CC>Armenia</color>, and were concluding their
conquest of Byzantine Syria. <color=#3366CC>Damascus</color> was the seat of the <color=#3366CC>Umayyad Caliphate</color>. By the end of 641 all of <color=#3366CC>Egypt</color> was in
Arab hands. A subsequent attempt to conquer the Nubian kingdom of <color=#3366CC>Makuria</color> was however repelled.
Maghreb
<color=#3366CC>Kairouan</color> in <color=#3366CC>Tunisia</color> was the first city founded by Muslims in the <color=#3366CC>Maghreb</color>. Arab general Uqba ibn Nafi erected the city
(in 670) and, in the same time, the <color=#3366CC>Great Mosque of Kairouan</color> considered as the oldest and most prestigious sanctuary
in the western Islamic world.
This part of Islamic territory has had independent governments during most of Islamic history. The <color=#3366CC>Idrisid</color> were the first
Arab rulers in the western <color=#3366CC>Maghreb</color> (Morocco), ruling from 788 to 985. The dynasty is named after its first <color=#3366CC>sultan</color> Idris I.
The <color=#3366CC>Almoravid dynasty</color> was a Berber dynasty from the <color=#3366CC>Sahara</color> flourished over a wide area of North-Western Africa and
the <color=#3366CC>Iberian Peninsula</color> during the 11th century. Under this dynasty the <color=#3366CC>Moorish</color> empire was extended over present-day
Morocco, Western Sahara, Mauritania, Gibraltar, Tlemcen (in Algeria) and a part of what is now <color=#3366CC>Senegal</color> and <color=#3366CC>Mali</color> in
the south, and Spain and Portugal in the north.
The <color=#3366CC>Almohad Dynasty</color> or "the Unitarians", were a Berber Muslim religious power which founded the fifth <color=#3366CC>Moorish</color>
dynasty in the 12th century, and conquered all Northern Africa as far as Egypt, together with Al-Andalus.
Horn of Africa
The history of Islam in the <color=#3366CC>Horn of Africa</color> is almost as old as the faith itself. Through extensive trade and social
interactions with their converted Muslim trading partners on the other side of the <color=#3366CC>Red Sea</color>, in the <color=#3366CC>Arabian peninsula</color>,
merchants and sailors in the Horn region gradually came under the influence of the new religion.
Early Islamic disciples fled to the port city of Zeila in modern-day northern <color=#3366CC>Somalia</color> to seek protection from the Quraysh
at the court of the <color=#3366CC>Emperor of Aksum</color>. Some of the Muslims that were granted protection are said to have then settled
in several parts of the Horn region to promote the religion. The victory of the Muslims over the Quraysh in the 7th
century had a significant impact on local merchants and sailors, as their trading partners in Arabia had by then all
adopted Islam, and the major trading routes in the <color=#3366CC>Mediterranean</color> and the Red Sea came under the sway of the <color=#3366CC>Muslim</color>
<color=#3366CC>Caliphs</color>. Instability in the Arabian peninsula saw further migrations of early Muslim families to the Somali seaboard.
These clans came to serve as catalysts, forwarding the faith to large parts of the Horn region.
East African coast
Islam came to the <color=#3366CC>Swahili coast</color> and South Eastern Africa along existing trade routes. They learned from them the
manners of the Muslims and this led to their conversion by the Muslim Arabs.
Local Islamic governments centered in Tanzania (then <color=#3366CC>Zanzibar</color>). The people of Zayd were Muslims that immigrated to
the region. In the pre-colonial period, the structure of Islamic authority here was held up through the <color=#3366CC>Ulema</color>
(wanawyuonis, in <color=#3366CC>Swahili language</color>). These leaders had some degree of authority over most of the Muslims in South
East Africa before territorial boundaries were established. The chief Qadi there was recognized for having the final
religious authority.
West Africa
Early contacts
Much of what is known about the early history of Islam in West Africa derives from <color=#3366CC>medieval</color> accounts written by Arab
and North African geographers and historians. After the rise of Islam in the seventh century, Islam was introduced into
West Africa and spread gradually from the 8th century onward along pre-existing <color=#3366CC>trans-Saharan trade</color> networks linking
the region with North Africa and the Mediterranean world. Early Muslim presence was largely confined to <color=#3366CC>merchant</color>
communities, clerics, and segments of the ruling elite in <color=#3366CC>Sahelian</color> towns, where literacy, commerce, and diplomacy
created favorable conditions for adoption. Rather than spreading through mass conversion, Islam initially functioned as
a religion of trade, scholarship, and administration.
From the 8th to the early 11th centuries, Islam spread gradually as a class religion, serving as the faith of merchant,
clerical, and administrative elites in <color=#3366CC>Sudanic</color> societies, while the broader population continued to follow indigenous
religious traditions. Political authorities often regulated Muslim influence by segregating Muslim communities or limiting
their participation in governance, a situation scholars describe as a stage of containment. Despite the expansion of
Muslim communities across the <color=#3366CC>Sahel</color>, political authority largely remained non-Islamic during this period.
Islamic states
Over the following centuries(11th–16th centuries), Islam became increasingly integrated into state structures across the
Sahel, as African rulers adopted the religion while continuing to govern populations with diverse religious practices.
This period corresponds to what scholars describe as a stage of mixing, during which Islamic beliefs and institutions
coexisted with, and were often adapted to, local religious and social traditions rather than replacing them entirely.
Mystical <color=#3366CC>Sufi</color> brotherhoods began to spread throughout West Africa. These orders played an important role in social
organization, education, and the diffusion of Islam, and they remained influential well into the 12th century.
One of the earliest known Islamic states in West Africa was the Kingdom of Takrur, located in the middle <color=#3366CC>Senegal River</color>
valley. Its ruler, War Dyābī, converted to Islam in the early 11th century and promoted stricter Islamic practices,
including the application of Islamic law, prior to the rise of the <color=#3366CC>Almoravids</color>. The <color=#3366CC>Mali Empire</color> incorporated Islamic
institutions into its political system, where Islam functioned primarily as a court religion rather than a uniformly practiced
popular faith. Its ruler, <color=#3366CC>Mansa Musa</color>, publicly demonstrated Mali's integration into the wider Islamic world through his
<color=#3366CC>pilgrimage to Mecca</color> in 1324. Similar forms of Islamic integration and recognition occurred in other <color=#3366CC>Sahelian</color> polities,
including the <color=#3366CC>Hausa city-states</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Kingdom of Kanem-Bornu</color> in present-day northern <color=#3366CC>Nigeria</color>.
The <color=#3366CC>Songhai Empire</color>, which succeeded Mali as the dominant power in the western Sahel, further expanded the role of
Islam in state administration and public life. Although many inhabitants continued to practice indigenous religious
systems, the Songhai state patronized Islamic institutions and sponsored mosques and centers of learning. Under
Songhai rule, <color=#3366CC>Timbuktu</color> emerged as a major center of Islamic scholarship during the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries,
attracting scholars from across North Africa and the broader Muslim world. The <color=#3366CC>Great Mosque of Djenné</color> in present-day
Mali exemplifies the architectural and religious significance of Islam in the region and remains the largest earthen
building in the world. After the Moroccan invasion of <color=#3366CC>Songhai</color>, <color=#3366CC>merchant</color>-scholars and religious elites dispersed from
urban centers such as Timbuktu, contributing to the spread of Islamic learning among rural and pastoral communities
across the <color=#3366CC>Sahara</color> and <color=#3366CC>Sahel</color>, many of which maintained indigenous practices.
Reform and resistance
From the 18th century onward, reformist movements emerged among West African Muslims who sought to eliminate
practices they regarded as <color=#3366CC>un-Islamic</color>, including the blending of Islamic and local religious traditions, and to enforce
Islamic law more fully. This period, often described as a stage of reform, was characterized by a series of <color=#3366CC>jihads</color> that
led to the establishment of new Islamic states.
In 1802, <color=#3366CC>Uthman dan Fodio</color>, a <color=#3366CC>Fulani</color> scholar, led a major jihad in <color=#3366CC>Hausaland</color> that overthrew existing rulers and led to
the creation of the <color=#3366CC>Sokoto Caliphate</color>. The new state centralized Muslim authority and introduced legal, educational, and
administrative reforms based on Islamic principles. Dan Fodio's movement inspired subsequent jihads, including that of
<color=#3366CC>Umar Tal</color> in the 1850s, who conquered several Bambara states, including the Ségou Empire and Kaarta in
Senegambia, and expanded the influence of the <color=#3366CC>Tijaniyyah</color> Sufi order into parts of West Africa, including northern
Nigeria.
These reformist jihads were followed in the 19th century by resistance movements and military campaigns against
European colonial expansion, including those led by <color=#3366CC>Samori Touré</color>, a Mandinka military strategist and founder of the
<color=#3366CC>Wassoulou Empire</color>, who opposed French forces until his capture in 1898; his successors were defeated in 1901. The
French occupation of Senegal subsequently reshaped Islamic practice in the region, as some leaders of Sufi orders
increasingly collaborated with colonial administrators.
Despite European colonial rule, Islam continued to spread across West Africa into the twentieth century, though its
expansion remained uneven. Muslim influence met resistance in regions with strong <color=#3366CC>kinship</color> systems, <color=#3366CC>ritual</color> institutions,
and <color=#3366CC>indigenous</color> religious traditions, particularly among Voltaic peoples. Some communities incorporated selected
Islamic practices without fully converting, while in others conversion occurred primarily through military conquest rather
than voluntary adoption. Where jihad states imposed Islam, these conversions were occasionally reversed following the
collapse of the regimes and during the colonial period, when traditional religious authorities and community institutions
regained authority.
By the late 19th and early 20th centuries, Islam had become a major religious force across much of West Africa,
particularly in the Sahel and savanna zones. Its historical development reflects a long process of adaptation,
negotiation, and reform rather than a single or uniform pattern of religious transformation.
East Asia
Indian subcontinent
On the <color=#3366CC>Indian subcontinent</color>, Islam first appeared in the southwestern tip of the peninsula, in today's <color=#3366CC>Kerala</color> state. Arabs
traded with Malabar even before the birth of Muhammad. Native legends say that a group of <color=#3366CC>Sahaba</color>, under Malik Ibn
Deenar, arrived on the Malabar Coast and preached Islam. According to that legend, the first mosque of India was built
by Second Chera King Cheraman Perumal, who accepted Islam and received the name Tajudheen. Historical records
suggest that the Cheraman Perumal Mosque was built in around 629.
Islamic rule first came to the Indian subcontinent in the 8th century, when Muhammad bin Qasim conquered <color=#3366CC>Sindh</color>,
though this was a short-lived consolidation of Indian territory. Islamic conquests expanded under <color=#3366CC>Mahmud of Ghazni</color> in
the 12th century CE, resulting in the establishment of the <color=#3366CC>Ghaznavid Empire</color> in the Indus River basin and the
subsequent prominence of <color=#3366CC>Lahore</color> as an eastern bastion of Ghaznavid culture and rule. Ghaznavid rule was eclipsed
by the <color=#3366CC>Ghurid Empire</color> of <color=#3366CC>Muhammad of Ghor</color> and Ghiyath al-Din Muhammad, whose domain under the conquests of
Muhammad bin Bakhtiyar Khalji extended until the <color=#3366CC>Bengal</color>, where Indian Islamic missionaries achieved their greatest
success in terms of dawah and number of converts to <color=#3366CC>Islam</color>. Qutb-ud-din Aybak conquered <color=#3366CC>Delhi</color> in 1206 and began
the reign of the <color=#3366CC>Delhi Sultanate</color>, a successive series of dynasties that synthesized Indian civilization with the wider
commercial and cultural networks of Africa and Eurasia, greatly increased demographic and economic growth in India
and deterred Mongol incursion into the prosperous <color=#3366CC>Indo-Gangetic plain</color> and enthroned one of the few female Muslim
rulers, Razia Sultana.
Many prominent sultanates and emirates administered various regions of the Indian subcontinent from the 13th to the

16th centuries, such as the <color=#3366CC>Qutb Shahi</color>, Gujarat, Kashmir, <color=#3366CC>Bengal</color>, <color=#3366CC>Bijapur</color> and <color=#3366CC>Bahmani Sultanates</color>, but none rivaled
the power and extensive reach of the <color=#3366CC>Mughal Empire</color> at its zenith. The Bengal Sultanate in particular was a major
global trading nation in the world, described by the Europeans to be the "richest country to trade with", while the Shah
Mir dynasty ensured the gradual conversion of Kashmiris to Islam.
Persian culture, art, language, cuisine and literature grew in prominence in India due to Islamic administration and the
immigration of soldiers, bureaucrats, merchants, Sufis, artists, poets, teachers and architects from Iran and Central
Asia, resulting in the early development of Indo-Persian culture.
Southeast Asia
Islam first reached Maritime Southeast Asia through traders from Mecca in the 7th century, particularly via the western
part of what is now <color=#3366CC>Indonesia</color>. Arab traders from Yemen already had a presence in Asia through trading and travelling
by sea, serving as intermediary traders to and from Europe and Africa. They traded not only Arabian goods but also
goods from Africa, India, and so on which included ivory, fragrances, spices, and gold.
According to T. W. Arnold in The Preaching of Islam, by the 2nd century of the <color=#3366CC>Islamic calendar</color>, Arab traders had been
trading with the inhabitants of <color=#3366CC>Ceylon</color>, modern-day Sri Lanka. The same argument has been told by Dr. B.H. Burger
and Dr. Mr. Prajudi in Sedjarah Ekonomis Sosiologis Indonesia (History of Socio Economic of Indonesia). According to
an atlas created by the geographer Al-Biruni (973–1048), the Indian or Indonesian Ocean used to be called the Persian
Ocean. After Western Imperialist rule, this name was changed to reflect the name used today; the Indian Ocean.
Soon, many <color=#3366CC>Sufi</color> missionaries translated classical Sufi literature from Arabic and Persian into <color=#3366CC>Malay</color>; a tangible product
of this is the <color=#3366CC>Jawi script</color>. Coupled with the composing of original <color=#3366CC>Islamic literature</color> in Malay, this led the way to the
transformation of Malay into an Islamic language. <color=#3366CC>Marco Polo</color> detected an Islamic kingdom in Perlak, <color=#3366CC>Sumatra</color> in 1292.
A powerful Islamic kingdom named Pasai was to grow from the north coast of <color=#3366CC>Sumatra</color>. The <color=#3366CC>Sultanate of Malacca</color> was
founded on the <color=#3366CC>Malay Peninsula</color> by <color=#3366CC>Parameswara</color>, a <color=#3366CC>Srivijayan</color> Prince.
Through trade and commerce, Islam then spread to <color=#3366CC>Borneo</color> and <color=#3366CC>Java</color>. By the late 15th century, Islam had been
introduced to the <color=#3366CC>Philippines</color> via the southern island of <color=#3366CC>Mindanao</color>. The foremost socio-cultural Muslim entities that
resulted from this are the Sultanate of Sulu and Sultanate of Maguindanao; Islamised kingdoms in the northern <color=#3366CC>Luzon</color>
island, such as the Kingdom of Maynila and the Kingdom of Tondo, were later conquered and Christianised with the
majority of the archipelago by Spanish colonisers beginning in the 16th century.
As Islam spread, societal changes developed from the individual conversions, and five centuries later it emerged as a
dominant cultural and political power in the region. Three main Muslim political powers emerged. The <color=#3366CC>Aceh Sultanate</color>
was the most important, controlling much of the area between Southeast Asia and India from its centre in northern
<color=#3366CC>Sumatra</color>. The Sultanate also attracted Sufi poets. The second Muslim power was the <color=#3366CC>Sultanate of Malacca</color> on the
Malay Peninsula. The Sultanate of Demak on Java was the third power, where the emerging Muslim forces defeated
the local <color=#3366CC>Majapahit</color> kingdom in the early 16th century. Although the sultanate managed to expand its territory
somewhat, its rule remained brief.
<color=#3366CC>Portuguese</color> forces captured Malacca in 1511 under naval general <color=#3366CC>Afonso de Albuquerque</color>. With Malacca subdued, the
<color=#3366CC>Aceh Sultanate</color> and <color=#3366CC>Bruneian Empire</color> established themselves as centres of Islam in Southeast Asia. The Sultanate's
territory, although vastly diminished, remains intact to this day as the modern state of <color=#3366CC>Brunei Darussalam</color>.
China
In China, four Sahabas (Sa'ad ibn abi Waqqas, Wahb Abu Kabcha, Jafar ibn Abu Talib and Jahsh ibn Riyab) preached

in 616/17 and onwards after following the <color=#3366CC>Chittagong</color>–Kamrup (<color=#3366CC>Sylhet</color>)–<color=#3366CC>Manipur</color> route after sailing from <color=#3366CC>Abyssinia</color> in
615/16. After conquering Persia in 636, Sa'ad ibn abi Waqqas went with Sa'id ibn Zaid, Qais ibn Sa'd and Hassan ibn
Thabit to China in 637 taking the complete Quran. Sa'ad ibn abi Waqqas headed for China for the third time in 650–51
after Caliph Uthman asked him to lead an embassy to China, which the Chinese emperor received.
Early Modern period
In the 15th and 16th centuries three major Muslim empires formed: the <color=#3366CC>Ottoman Empire</color> in Anatolia, the <color=#3366CC>Balkans</color>, the

<color=#3366CC>Middle East</color>, and <color=#3366CC>North Africa</color>; the <color=#3366CC>Safavid Empire</color> in <color=#3366CC>Greater Iran</color>; and the <color=#3366CC>Mughal Empire</color> in <color=#3366CC>South Asia</color>. These
imperial powers were made possible by the discovery and exploitation of <color=#3366CC>gunpowder</color> and more efficient administration.
Ottoman Empire
According to Ottoman historiography, the legitimation of a ruler is attributed to Sheikh Edebali who interpreted a dream
of <color=#3366CC>Osman Gazi</color> as God's legitimation of his reign. Since <color=#3366CC>Murad I</color>'s conquest of Edirne in 1362, the caliphate was
claimed by the Turkish sultans of the empire. During the period of Ottoman growth, claims on caliphal authority were
recognized in 1517 as <color=#3366CC>Selim I</color> became the "Custodian of the Two Holy Mosques" in Mecca and Medina through the
conquering and unification of Muslim lands, strengthening their claim to the caliphate in the <color=#3366CC>Muslim world</color>.
The Seljuq Turks declined in the second half of the 13th century, after the Mongol invasion of Anatolia. This resulted in
the establishment of multiple Turkish principalities, known as <color=#3366CC>beyliks</color>. <color=#3366CC>Osman I</color>, the founder of the <color=#3366CC>Ottoman dynasty</color>,
assumed leadership of one of these principalities (Söğüt) at the end of the 13th century, succeeding his father Ertuğrul.
Osman I afterwards led it in a series of battles with the Byzantine Empire. By 1331, the Ottoman Turks had captured
Nicaea, the former Byzantine capital, under the leadership of Osman's son and successor, Orhan I. Victory at the Battle
of Kosovo against the Serbian Empire in 1389 then facilitated their expansion into Europe. The Ottomans were
established in the Balkans and Anatolia by the time Bayezid I ascended to power in the same year, now at the helm of
a growing empire.
Growth halted when Mongol warlord <color=#3366CC>Timur</color> (also known as "Tamerlane") captured Bayezid I in the <color=#3366CC>Battle of Ankara</color> in
1402, beginning the Ottoman Interregnum. This episode was characterized by the division of the Ottoman territory
amongst Bayezid I's sons, who submitted to Timurid authority. When a number of Ottoman territories regained
independent status, ruin for the Empire loomed. However, the empire recovered as the youngest son of Bayezid I,
Mehmed I, waged offensive campaigns against his ruling brothers, thereby reuniting <color=#3366CC>Asia Minor</color> and declaring himself
sultan in 1413. Around 1512 the Ottoman naval fleet developed under the rule of <color=#3366CC>Selim I</color>, such that the Ottoman Turks
were able to challenge the <color=#3366CC>Republic of Venice</color>, a <color=#3366CC>naval power</color> which established its thalassocracy alongside the other
Italian <color=#3366CC>maritime republics</color> upon the Mediterranean Region. They also attempted to reconquer the Balkans. By the time
of Mehmed I's grandson, <color=#3366CC>Mehmed II</color> (ruled 1444–1446; 1451–1481), the Ottomans could lay siege to <color=#3366CC>Constantinople</color>,
the capital of Byzantium. A factor in this siege was the use of <color=#3366CC>muskets</color> and large <color=#3366CC>cannons</color> introduced by the Ottomans.
The Byzantine fortress <color=#3366CC>succumbed</color> in 1453, after 54 days of siege. Without its capital the Byzantine Empire
disintegrated. The future successes of the Ottomans and later empires would depend upon the exploitation of
<color=#3366CC>gunpowder</color>.
In the early 16th century, the Shiite <color=#3366CC>Safavid dynasty</color> assumed control in Persia under the leadership of Shah <color=#3366CC>Ismail I</color>,
defeating the ruling Turcoman federation <color=#3366CC>Aq Qoyunlu</color> (also called the "White Sheep Turkomans") in 1501. The Ottoman
sultan <color=#3366CC>Selim I</color> sought to repel Safavid expansion, challenging and defeating them at the Battle of Chaldiran in 1514.
Selim I also deposed the ruling Mamluks in Egypt, absorbing their territories in 1517. <color=#3366CC>Suleiman I</color> (nicknamed "Suleiman
the Magnificent"), Selim I's successor, took advantage of the diversion of Safavid focus to the Uzbeks on the eastern
frontier and recaptured Baghdad, which had fallen under Safavid control. Despite this, Safavid power remained
substantial, rivalling the Ottomans. Suleiman I advanced deep into Hungary following the <color=#3366CC>Battle of Mohács</color> in 1526 –
reaching as far as the gates of Vienna thereafter, and signed a Franco-Ottoman alliance with <color=#3366CC>Francis I of France</color>
against <color=#3366CC>Charles V</color> of the <color=#3366CC>Holy Roman Empire</color> 10 years later. While Suleiman I's rule (1520–1566) is often identified as
the apex of Ottoman power, the empire continued to remain powerful and influential until a relative fall in its military
strength in the second half of the 18th century.
Safavid Empire
The Shīīte <color=#3366CC>Safavid dynasty</color> rose to power in <color=#3366CC>Tabriz</color> in 1501 and later conquered the rest of Iran. They were of mixed
ancestry, originally <color=#3366CC>Kurdish</color>, but during their rule intermarried with Turcomans, Georgians, <color=#3366CC>Circassians</color>, and Pontic
Greeks. The Safavid dynasty had its origin in the Safavid order of <color=#3366CC>Sufism</color>, while the Iranian population was largely
composed by <color=#3366CC>Sunni Muslims</color>. After their defeat at the hands of the Sunni Ottomans at the Battle of Chaldiran, to unite
the Persians behind him, Shah <color=#3366CC>Ismail I</color> made conversion mandatory for the largely Sunni population of Iran to the
<color=#3366CC>Twelver sect of Shīa Islam</color> so that he could get them to fight against the Sunni Ottomans.
This resulted in the <color=#3366CC>Safavid conversion of Iran to Shīa Islam</color>. Iranian <color=#3366CC>Zaydis</color>, the largest group amongst the Shīa
Muslims before the <color=#3366CC>Safavid rule</color>, were also forced to convert to the <color=#3366CC>Twelver</color> denomination of Shīa Islam. The Zaydis at
that time subscribed to the <color=#3366CC>Hanafi</color> <color=#3366CC>jurisprudence</color>, as did most Sunnis, and there were good relations between them.
<color=#3366CC>Abu Hanifah</color> and <color=#3366CC>Zayd ibn Ali</color> were also very good friends. The Safavid dynasty from Azarbaijan ruled from 1501 to
1736; they <color=#3366CC>established Twelver Shīīsm as the official religion of Safavid Iran</color> and united its provinces under a single
sovereignty, thereby reigniting the <color=#3366CC>Persian identity</color>.
In 1524, Tahmasp I acceded to the throne, initiating a revival of the arts. Carpetmaking became a major industry. The
tradition of <color=#3366CC>Persian miniature</color> painting in manuscripts reached its peak, until Tahmasp turned to strict religious
observance in middle age, prohibiting the consumption of <color=#3366CC>alcohol</color> and hashish and removing <color=#3366CC>casinos</color>, <color=#3366CC>taverns</color>, and
<color=#3366CC>brothels</color>. Tahmasp's nephew Ibrahim Mirza continued to patronize a last flowering of the arts until he was murdered,
after which many artists were recruited by the Mughal dynasty.
Tahmasp's grandson, <color=#3366CC>Shah Abbas I</color>, restored the shrine of the eighth Twelver Shīīte Imam, <color=#3366CC>Ali al-Ridha</color> at <color=#3366CC>Mashhad</color>,
and restored the dynastic shrine at <color=#3366CC>Ardabil</color>. Both shrines received jewelry, fine manuscripts, and Chinese porcelains.
Abbas moved the capital to <color=#3366CC>Isfahan</color>, revived old ports, and established thriving trade with Europeans. Amongst Abbas'
most visible cultural achievements was the construction of <color=#3366CC>Naqsh-e Jahan Square</color> ("Design of the World"). The plaza,
located near a Friday mosque, covered 20 acre. The <color=#3366CC>Safavid dynasty</color> was toppled in 1722 by the Hotaki dynasty, which
ended their forceful conversion of Sunni areas to Twelver Shīīsm.
Mughal Empire
Mughal Empire was a power that comprised almost all of <color=#3366CC>South Asia</color>, founded in 1526. It was established and ruled by
the Timurid dynasty, with Turco-Mongol <color=#3366CC>Chagatai</color> roots from <color=#3366CC>Central Asia</color>, claiming direct descent from both <color=#3366CC>Genghis</color>

<color=#3366CC>Khan</color> (through his son Chagatai Khan) and <color=#3366CC>Timur</color>, and with significant <color=#3366CC>Indian</color> and <color=#3366CC>Persian</color> ancestry through marriage
alliances; the first two Mughal emperors had both parents of Central Asian ancestry, while successive emperors were
of predominantly Indo-Persian ancestry. The dynasty was Indo-Persian in culture, combining Persianate culture with
local <color=#3366CC>Indian cultural</color> influences visible in its court culture and administrative customs.
The beginning of the empire is conventionally dated to the victory by its founder <color=#3366CC>Babur</color> over Ibrahim Lodi, the last ruler
of the <color=#3366CC>Delhi Sultanate</color>, in the <color=#3366CC>First Battle of Panipat</color> (1526). During the reign of <color=#3366CC>Humayun</color>, the successor of Babur, the
empire was briefly interrupted by the Sur Empire established by <color=#3366CC>Sher Shah Suri</color>, who re-established the Grand Trunk
Road across the northern Indian subcontinent, initiated the rupee currency system and developed much of the
foundations of the effective administration of Mughal rule. The "classic period" of the Mughal Empire began in 1556,
with the ascension of <color=#3366CC>Akbar</color> to the throne. Some Rajput kingdoms continued to pose a significant threat to the Mughal
dominance of northwestern India, but most of them were subdued by Akbar. All Mughal emperors were <color=#3366CC>Muslims</color>;
Akbar, however, propounded a syncretic religion in the latter part of his life called Dīn-i Ilāhī, as recorded in historical
books like Ain-i-Akbari and Dabistān-i Mazāhib. The Mughal Empire did not try to intervene in native societies during
most of its existence, rather co-opting and pacifying them through concilliatory administrative practices and a syncretic,
inclusive ruling elite, leading to more systematic, centralized and uniform rule. Traditional and newly coherent social
groups in northern and western India, such as the <color=#3366CC>Marathas</color>, the Rajputs, the <color=#3366CC>Pashtuns</color>, the Hindu Jats and the Sikhs,
gained military and governing ambitions during Mughal rule which, through collaboration or adversity, gave them both
recognition and military experience.
The reign of <color=#3366CC>Shah Jahan</color> (1628–1658) represented the height of Mughal architecture, with famous monuments such as
the <color=#3366CC>Taj Mahal</color>, Moti Masjid, <color=#3366CC>Red Fort</color>, Jama Masjid and Lahore Fort being constructed during his reign.
The <color=#3366CC>sharia</color> reign of <color=#3366CC>Muhammad Auranzgeb</color> witnessed the establishment of the Fatawa-e-Alamgiri. Muslim India
became the world's largest economy, valued 25% of world <color=#3366CC>GDP</color>. Its richest province, Bengal Subah, which was a world
leading economy and had better conditions than 18th century <color=#3366CC>Western Europe</color>, showed signs of the <color=#3366CC>Industrial</color>
<color=#3366CC>Revolution</color>, through the emergence of the period of proto-industrialization. Numerous conflicts such as the
Anglo-Mughal War were also witnessed.
After the death of <color=#3366CC>Aurangzeb</color>, which marks the end of Medieval India and beginning of the European colonialism in
India, internal dissatisfaction arose due to the weakness of the empire's administrative and economic systems, leading
to its break-up and declarations of independence of its former provinces by the <color=#3366CC>Nawab of Bengal</color>, the Nawab of Awadh,
the Nizam of Hyderabad, the major economic and military power known as <color=#3366CC>Kingdom of Mysore</color> ruled by <color=#3366CC>Tipu Sultan</color>
and other small states. In 1739, the Mughals were crushingly defeated in the Battle of Karnal by the forces of <color=#3366CC>Nader</color>
<color=#3366CC>Shah</color>, the founder of the Afsharid dynasty in Persia, and Delhi was sacked and looted, drastically accelerating their
decline.
In 1757, the <color=#3366CC>East India Company</color> overtook Bengal Subah at the <color=#3366CC>Battle of Plassey</color>. By the mid-18th century, the
<color=#3366CC>Marathas</color> had routed Mughal armies and won over several Mughal provinces from the <color=#3366CC>Punjab</color> to <color=#3366CC>Bengal</color>.
<color=#3366CC>Tipu Sultan</color>'s <color=#3366CC>Kingdom of Mysore</color> based in <color=#3366CC>South India</color>, which witnessed partial establishment of <color=#3366CC>sharia</color> based
economic and military policies i.e. Fathul Mujahidin, replaced Bengal ruled by the <color=#3366CC>Nawabs of Bengal</color> as <color=#3366CC>South Asia</color>'s
foremost economic territory. The Anglo-Mysore Wars were fought between <color=#3366CC>Hyder Ali</color>, his son <color=#3366CC>Tipu</color> and their <color=#3366CC>French</color>
allies, including <color=#3366CC>Napoleon</color> Bonaparte, and the <color=#3366CC>East India Company</color>. <color=#3366CC>Rocket artillery</color> and the world's first iron-cased
rockets, the Mysorean rockets, were used during the war and the <color=#3366CC>Jihad</color> based Fathul Mujahidin was compiled.
During the following century Mughal power had become severely limited, and the last emperor, <color=#3366CC>Bahadur Shah II</color>, had
authority over only the city of Shahjahanabad. Bahadur issued a firman supporting the <color=#3366CC>Indian Rebellion of 1857</color>.
Consequent to the rebellion's defeat he was tried by the <color=#3366CC>East India Company</color> authorities for treason, imprisoned, and
exiled to <color=#3366CC>Rangoon</color>. The last remnants of the empire were formally taken over by the British, and the <color=#3366CC>British parliament</color>
passed the Government of India Act to enable the Crown formally to <color=#3366CC>nationalize</color> the East India Company and assume
direct control of India in the form of the new <color=#3366CC>British Raj</color>.
Modern period
Ottoman Empire partition
By the end of the 19th century, the Ottoman Empire had declined. The decision to back <color=#3366CC>Germany</color> in <color=#3366CC>World War I</color> meant
they shared the <color=#3366CC>Central Powers</color>' defeat in that war. The defeat led to the overthrow of the Ottomans by Turkish
nationalists led by the victorious general of the <color=#3366CC>Battle of Gallipoli</color>: <color=#3366CC>Mustafa Kemal</color>, who became known to his people as
Atatürk, "Father of the Turks." Atatürk was credited with renegotiating the treaty of Sèvres (1920) which ended Turkey's
involvement in the war and establishing the modern <color=#3366CC>Republic of Turkey</color>, which was recognized by the <color=#3366CC>Allies</color> in the
Treaty of Lausanne (1923). Atatürk went on to implement an ambitious program of modernization that emphasized
economic development and <color=#3366CC>secularization</color>. He transformed Turkish culture to reflect European laws, adopted <color=#3366CC>Arabic</color>
<color=#3366CC>numerals</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Latin script</color>, separated the religious establishment from the state, and emancipated woman—even giving
them the right to vote in parallel with <color=#3366CC>women's suffrage</color> in the west.
During the First World War, the Allies cooperated with Arab partisans against the Ottoman Empire, both groups being
united in opposition to a common enemy. The most prominent example of this was during the <color=#3366CC>Arab Revolt</color>, when the
British, led by secret intelligence agent <color=#3366CC>T. E. Lawrence</color>—better known as "Lawrence of Arabia" cooperated with Arab
<color=#3366CC>guerillas</color> against the Ottoman forces, eventually securing the withdrawal of all Ottoman troops from the region by 1918.
Following the end of the war, the vast majority of former Ottoman territory outside of Asia Minor was handed over to the
victorious European powers as <color=#3366CC>protectorates</color>. However, many Arabs were left dismayed by the <color=#3366CC>Balfour Declaration</color>,
which directly contradicted the McMahon–Hussein Correspondence publicized only a year earlier. Ottoman successor

states include today's <color=#3366CC>Albania</color>, <color=#3366CC>Bosnia and Herzegovina</color>, <color=#3366CC>Bulgaria</color>, Egypt, Greece, Iraq, <color=#3366CC>Israel</color>, Lebanon, <color=#3366CC>Romania</color>,

<color=#3366CC>Saudi Arabia</color>, <color=#3366CC>Serbia</color>, <color=#3366CC>Syria</color>, <color=#3366CC>Jordan</color>, Turkey, Balkan states, North Africa and the north shore of the <color=#3366CC>Black Sea</color>.
Arab–Israeli conflict
The Arab–Israeli conflict spans about a century of political tensions and open hostilities. It involves the establishment of

the modern <color=#3366CC>State of Israel</color> as a <color=#3366CC>Jewish</color> <color=#3366CC>nation state</color>, the consequent <color=#3366CC>displacement</color> of the Palestinian people and <color=#3366CC>Jewish</color>
<color=#3366CC>exodus from Arab and Muslim countries</color>, as well as the adverse relationship between the <color=#3366CC>Arab world</color> and the State of
Israel (see: <color=#3366CC>Israeli–Palestinian conflict</color>). Despite at first involving only the Arab states bordering Israel, animosity has
also developed between Israel and other predominantly <color=#3366CC>Muslim-majority countries</color>.
The State of Israel came into existence on 14 May 1948 as a polity to serve as the homeland for the Jewish people. It
was also defined in its declaration of independence as a "Jewish state", a term that also appeared in the United Nations
Partition Plan for British Palestine in 1947. The related term of "Jewish and democratic state" dates from a 1992
legislation by Israel's Knesset.

The <color=#3366CC>Six-Day War</color> of 5–10 June 1967, was fought between <color=#3366CC>Israel</color> and the neighbouring states of <color=#3366CC>Egypt</color>, <color=#3366CC>Jordan</color>, and
<color=#3366CC>Syria</color>. The Arab countries closed the <color=#3366CC>Suez Canal</color> and it was followed in May 1970 by the closure of the "tapline" from
<color=#3366CC>Saudi Arabia</color> through Syria to <color=#3366CC>Lebanon</color>. These developments had the effect of increasing the importance of <color=#3366CC>petroleum</color>
in <color=#3366CC>Libya</color>, which is a short (and canal-free) shipping distance from Europe. In 1970, Occidental Petroleum broke with
other oil companies and accepted the Arab demands for price increases.
In October 1973, a new war between Israel and its Muslim neighbours, known as the <color=#3366CC>Yom Kippur War</color>, broke out just
as the oil companies began meeting with the Organization of Arab Petroleum Exporting Countries (OAPEC). Its leaders
had been emboldened by the success of <color=#3366CC>Sadat's campaigns</color> and the war strengthened their unity. In response to the
emergency resupply effort by the Western Bloc that enabled Israel to put up a resistance against the Egyptian and
Syrian forces, the Arab world imposed the <color=#3366CC>1973 oil embargo</color> against the United States and Western Europe. Faisal
agreed that Saudi Arabia would use some of its oil wealth to finance the "front-line states", those that bordered Israel, in
their struggle. The centrality of petroleum, the <color=#3366CC>Arab–Israeli conflict</color>, political and economic instability, and uncertainty
about the future remain constant features of the politics of the region.
Many countries, individuals, and <color=#3366CC>non-governmental organizations</color> elsewhere in the world feel involved in this conflict for
reasons such as cultural and religious ties with Islam, <color=#3366CC>Arab culture</color>, <color=#3366CC>Christianity</color>, <color=#3366CC>Judaism</color>, Jewish culture, or for
ideological, <color=#3366CC>human rights</color>, or strategic reasons. Although some consider the Arab–Israeli conflict a part of (or a
precursor to) a wider clash of civilizations between the <color=#3366CC>Western world</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Muslim world</color>, others oppose this view.
Animosity emanating from this conflict has caused numerous attacks on supporters (or perceived supporters) of each
side by supporters of the other side in many countries around the world.
Other Islamic affairs

In 1979 the <color=#3366CC>Iranian revolution</color> transformed <color=#3366CC>Iran</color> from a constitutional monarchy to a <color=#3366CC>populist</color> <color=#3366CC>theocratic</color> Islamic republic
under the rule of Ayatollah <color=#3366CC>Ruhollah Khomeini</color>, a Shi'i Muslim cleric and marja. Following the Revolution, a new
constitution was approved and a referendum established the government, electing Ruhollah Khomeini as Supreme
Leader. During the following two years, liberals, leftists, and Islamic groups fought each other, and the Islamics
captured power.
The development of the two opposite fringes, the <color=#3366CC>Safavid conversion of Iran to Shia Islam</color>, the Twelver Shia version,
and its reinforcement by the <color=#3366CC>Iranian revolution</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Salafi</color> in Saudi Arabia, coupled with the Iran–Saudi Arabia
relations resulted in these governments using sectarian conflict to enhance their political interests. Gulf states such as
Saudi Arabia and Kuwait (despite being hostile to Iraq) encouraged <color=#3366CC>Saddam Hussein</color> to invade Iran, which resulted in
the <color=#3366CC>Iran–Iraq War</color>, as they feared that an Islamic revolution would take place within their own borders. Certain Iranian
exiles also helped convince Saddam that if he invaded, the fledgling Islamic republic would quickly collapse.
Urtica dioica
Urtica dioica, often known as common nettle, burn nettle, stinging nettle, nettle leaf, or just a nettle or stinger, is a
<color=#3366CC>herbaceous</color> perennial <color=#3366CC>flowering plant</color> in the family <color=#3366CC>Urticaceae</color>. Originally native to Europe, much of temperate Asia and
western North Africa, it is now found worldwide.
The species is divided into six <color=#3366CC>subspecies</color>, five of which have many hollow stinging hairs called trichomes on the leaves
and stems, which act like <color=#3366CC>hypodermic needles</color>, injecting histamine and other chemicals that produce a stinging
sensation upon contact ("contact urticaria", a form of contact dermatitis).
The plant has a long history of use as a source for <color=#3366CC>traditional medicine</color>, food, tea, and <color=#3366CC>textile</color> raw material in ancient
(such as <color=#3366CC>Saxon</color>) and modern societies.
Description
Urtica dioica is a dioecious, <color=#3366CC>herbaceous</color>, and perennial plant. It grows to 3 to 7 ft tall in the summer and dying down to
the ground in winter. It has widely spreading <color=#3366CC>rhizomes</color> and <color=#3366CC>stolons</color>, which are bright yellow, as are the roots. The soft,
green <color=#3366CC>leaves</color> are 1 to 6 in long and are borne oppositely on an erect, wiry, green stem. The leaves have a strongly
serrated margin, a cordate base, and an acuminate tip with a terminal leaf tooth longer than adjacent laterals. It bears
small, greenish or brownish, numerous flowers in dense axillary inflorescences.
The leaves and stems are very hairy with non-stinging hairs, and in most subspecies, also bear many stinging hairs
(trichomes or spicules), whose tips come off when touched, transforming the hair into a needle that can inject several
chemicals causing a painful sting or paresthesia, giving the species its common names: stinging nettle, burn-nettle,
burn-weed, or burn-hazel.
Taxonomy
Credit for the scientific naming of Urtica dioica is given to <color=#3366CC>Carl Linnaeus</color>, who published it in Species Plantarum in
1753. The <color=#3366CC>taxonomy</color> of Urtica species is confused, and sources are likely to use a variety of systematic names for
these plants. Until 2014 there was broad consensus that the nettles native to the Americas, now classified as Urtica
gracilis, were <color=#3366CC>subspecies</color> of U. dioica. However, in that year the paper "Weeding the Nettles II" was published in the
journal Phytotaxa demonstrating the genetic distinctness of New World nettles. As of 2023 Plants of the World Online
(POWO) recognises U. gracilis as a distinct species while the USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service PLANTS
database continues to list it as U. dioica subsp. gracilis, as does the Flora of North America.
As of 2023 POWO recognises 11 subspecies or varieties of U. dioica:
• Urtica dioica subsp. afghanica Chrtek, from southwestern and central Asia, sometimes has stinging hairs or is
sometimes hairless.
• Urtica dioica subsp. dioica (European stinging nettle), from Europe, Asia, and northern Africa, has stinging hairs.
• Urtica dioica subsp. gansuensis C.J.Chen, from eastern Asia (China), has stinging hairs.
• Urtica dioica var. glabrata (Clem.) Asch. & Graebn.
• Urtica dioica var. hispida (Lam. ex DC.) Tausch ex Ott

Etymology
Urtica is derived from a <color=#3366CC>Latin</color> word meaning 'sting'.
Dioica is derived from <color=#3366CC>Greek</color>, meaning 'of two houses' (having separate staminate and pistillate plants; dioecious).
Distribution and habitat
U. dioica is considered to be native to Europe, much of temperate <color=#3366CC>Asia</color> and western <color=#3366CC>North Africa</color>. It is abundant in
<color=#3366CC>northern Europe</color> and much of Asia, usually found in the countryside. It is less widespread in southern Europe and north
Africa, where it is restricted by its need for moist soil, but is still common. It has been introduced to many other parts of
the world. In North America, it is widely distributed in <color=#3366CC>Canada</color> and the United States, where it is found in every province
and state except for <color=#3366CC>Hawaii</color>, and also can be found in northernmost <color=#3366CC>Mexico</color>. It grows in abundance in the <color=#3366CC>Pacific</color>
<color=#3366CC>Northwest</color>, especially in places where annual rainfall is high. The European subspecies has been introduced into
Australia, North America and <color=#3366CC>South America</color>.
In Europe, nettles have a strong association with human habitation and buildings. The presence of nettles may indicate
the site of a long-abandoned building, and can also indicate <color=#3366CC>soil fertility</color>. Human and animal waste may be responsible
for elevated levels of <color=#3366CC>phosphate</color> and <color=#3366CC>nitrogen</color> in the soil, providing an ideal environment for nettles.
Ecology
Nettles are the <color=#3366CC>larval</color> food plant for several species of <color=#3366CC>butterflies</color> in the <color=#3366CC>Nymphalidae</color> family, such as the peacock
butterfly, comma (Polygonia c-album), and the small tortoiseshell. It is also eaten by the larvae of some <color=#3366CC>moths</color> including
angle shades, buff ermine, dot moth, the flame, the gothic, grey chi, grey pug, lesser broad-bordered yellow underwing,
mouse moth, setaceous Hebrew character, and small angle shades. The <color=#3366CC>roots</color> are sometimes eaten by the larva of the
ghost moth (Hepialus humuli).
It is a known host to the <color=#3366CC>pathogenic</color> fungus Phoma herbarum.
Stinging nettle is particularly found as an understory plant in wetter environments, but it is also found in meadows.
Although nutritious, it is not widely eaten by either wildlife or livestock, presumably because of the sting. It spreads by
abundant seeds and also by rhizomes, and is often able to survive and re-establish quickly after fire.
Cultivation
Field
Sowing and planting
Three cultivation techniques can be used for the stinging nettle: 1) direct sowing, 2) growing seedlings in nurseries with
subsequent transplantation and 3) vegetative propagation via stolons or head cuttings.
• Direct sowing: The <color=#3366CC>seedbed</color> should have a loose and fine structure, but should be reconsolidated using a packer
roller imminently prior to sowing. Sowing time can be either in autumn or in spring. Seed density should be 6
kilograms/hectare with row spacing of 30 cm and 42–50 cm in autumn and spring, respectively. The disadvantage
of direct sowing is that it usually leads to incomplete plant coverage. This drawback can be mitigated by covering
the seedbed with a transparent perforated foil in order to improve seed germination. Further, weed control can be
problematic as the stinging nettle has a slow seedling development time.
• Growing seedlings: For this technique pre-germinated seeds are sown between mid-/end-February and beginning
of April and grown in <color=#3366CC>nurseries</color>. Seedlings are grown in tuffs with 3–5 plants/tuff and a seed density of 1.2–1.6
kg/1000 tuffs. Faster germination is achieved by alternating high temperature during daytime (30 °C for 8 h) and
lower temperature during nighttime (20 °C for 16 h). Before transplanting, the seedlings should be fertilised and
acclimated to cold temperatures. Transplantation should start around Mid-April with row spacing of 42 – 50 cm and
plant spacing within rows of 25–30 cm.
• Vegetative propagation: Stolons (with several buds) of 10 cm should be planted from mid-April in a depth of 5 – 7
cm. Head cuttings are grown in <color=#3366CC>nurseries</color> starting between mid-May and mid-June. Growing tips with two leaf pairs
are cut from the mother plant and treated with root-growth inducing hormones. Transplantation can be delayed in
comparison to the growing seedling technique.
Greenhouse
The stinging nettle can also be grown in controlled-environment agriculture systems, such as soil-less medium
cultivations or aeroponics, which may achieve higher yields, standardise quality, and reduce harvesting costs and
contamination.
Sting and treatment
Urtica dioica produces its <color=#3366CC>inflammatory</color> effect on skin (a stinging, burning sensation often called "contact urticaria") both
by impaling the skin via spicules – causing mechanical irritation – and by <color=#3366CC>biochemical</color> irritants, such as histamine,
<color=#3366CC>serotonin</color>, and <color=#3366CC>acetylcholine</color>, among other chemicals. In especially sensitive individuals, anti-itch drugs, usually in the
form of creams containing <color=#3366CC>antihistamines</color> or <color=#3366CC>hydrocortisone</color>, may provide relief from nettle <color=#3366CC>dermatitis</color>, though the
symptoms are essentially self-resolving and typically only last about 10 minutes. In some cases, durations of 12 hours
or more have been observed. The term contact urticaria has a wider use in <color=#3366CC>dermatology</color>, involving dermatitis caused by
various skin irritants and <color=#3366CC>pathogens</color>.
Docks, especially Rumex obtusifolius (the broad-leaf dock) often grow in similar environments to stinging nettles and
are regarded as a <color=#3366CC>folk remedy</color> to counteract the sting of a nettle, although there is no evidence of any chemical effect. It
may be that the act of rubbing a dock leaf against a nettle sting acts as a distracting counterstimulation, or that belief in
the dock's effect provides a <color=#3366CC>placebo effect</color>.
Uses
Culinary
U. dioica has a flavour similar to <color=#3366CC>spinach</color> when cooked. Young plants are harvested by many <color=#3366CC>Native American</color>
communities and are cooked and eaten in spring when other food plants are scarce. Soaking stinging nettles in water
or cooking removes the stinging chemicals from the plant, which allows them to be handled and eaten without injury.
After the stinging nettle enters its flowering and seed-setting stages, the leaves develop gritty particles called cystoliths.
Many sources claim consumption of these can irritate the kidneys and urinary tract, but there is no medical evidence to
support this claim. Cystoliths are made of <color=#3366CC>calcium carbonate</color>, and will not dissolve when boiled. Leaves harvested
post-flowering must have their cystoliths broken down by <color=#3366CC>acid</color>, as in the <color=#3366CC>fermentation process</color>. In its peak season, nettle
contains up to 25% protein, dry weight, which is high for a leafy green vegetable. The leaves are also dried and may
then be used to make a <color=#3366CC>herbal tea</color>, as can also be done with the nettle's flowers.
Nettles can be used in a variety of recipes, such as polenta, <color=#3366CC>pesto</color>, and purée. Nettle soup is a common use of the
plant, particularly in Northern and Eastern <color=#3366CC>Europe</color>.
Nettles are sometimes used in cheesemaking, such as for Cornish Yarg and as a flavouring in varieties of Gouda.

Nettles are used in <color=#3366CC>Albania</color>, <color=#3366CC>Montenegro</color>, <color=#3366CC>Serbia</color>, <color=#3366CC>North Macedonia</color> and <color=#3366CC>Bosnia and Herzegovina</color> as part of the dough
filling for the börek pastry. The top baby leaves are selected and simmered, and then mixed with other ingredients such
as herbs and rice, before being used as a filling between dough layers. Similarly, in <color=#3366CC>Greece</color> the tender leaves are often
used, after simmering, as a filling for hortopita, which is similar to spanakopita, but with wild greens rather than spinach
for filling.
Young nettles can also be used to make an <color=#3366CC>alcoholic drink</color>.
Competitive eating
In the United Kingdom, an annual World Nettle Eating Championship draws thousands of people to <color=#3366CC>Dorset</color>, where
competitors attempt to eat as much of the raw plant as possible. Competitors are given 60 cm stalks of the plant, from
which they strip the leaves and eat them. Whoever strips and eats the most stinging nettle leaves in a fixed time is the
winner. The competition dates back to 1986, when two neighbouring farmers attempted to settle a dispute about which
had the worst infestation of nettles, and one of them said to the other, "I'll eat any nettle of yours that's longer than
mine."
Traditional medicine
As <color=#3366CC>Old English</color> stiþe and wergulu, nettle is one of the nine plants invoked in the pagan Anglo-Saxon Nine Herbs
Charm, recorded in 10th-century <color=#3366CC>traditional medicine</color>. Nettle was believed to be a galactagogue – a substance that
promotes <color=#3366CC>lactation</color>. Urtication, or flogging with nettles, is the process of deliberately applying stinging nettles to the skin
to provoke <color=#3366CC>inflammation</color>; an agent thus used was considered to be a rubefacient (something that causes redness),
used as a <color=#3366CC>folk remedy</color> to supposedly treat rheumatism.
Chastisement
In indigenous justice systems in <color=#3366CC>Ecuador</color>, urtication was used as punishment for severe crimes in 2010. The sentenced
perpetrator of a crime was flogged with stinging nettle, in public, naked, whilst being showered with freezing cold ice
water.
Textiles and fibre
Nettle stems contain a bast fibre that has been traditionally used for the same purposes as <color=#3366CC>linen</color> and is produced by a
similar retting process. Unlike <color=#3366CC>cotton</color>, nettles grow easily without <color=#3366CC>pesticides</color>. The fibres are coarser, however.
Historically, nettles have been used to make clothing for almost 3,000 years, as ancient nettle textiles from the Bronze
Age have been found in Denmark. It is widely believed that German Army uniforms were almost all made from nettle
during World War I due to a shortage of cotton, although there is little evidence to support this. More recently,
companies in Austria, Germany, and Italy have started to produce commercial nettle textiles.
The fibre content in nettle shows a high variability and reaches from below 1% to 17%. Under middle-European
conditions, stems yield typically between 45 and 55 dt / ha (decitons per hectare), which is comparable to <color=#3366CC>flax</color> stem
yield. Due to the variable fibre content, the fibre yields vary between 0.2 and 7 dt / ha, but the yields are normally in the
range between 2 and 4 dt / ha. Fibre varieties are normally cloning varieties and therefore planted from vegetative
propagated plantlets. Direct seeding is possible, but leads to great heterogeneity in maturity.
Nettles may be used as a <color=#3366CC>dye-stuff</color>, producing yellow from the roots, or yellowish green from the leaves.
Feed
Nutrient contents
Fresh leaves contain approximately 82.4% water, 17.6% dry matter, 5.5% protein, 0.7 to 3.3% fat, and 7.1%
carbohydrates. Mature leaves contain about 40% - linolenic acid, a valuable omega-3 acid. For exact fatty acid
contents see Table 1. Seeds contain much more fatty acid than leaves.
Minerals (Ca, K, Mg, P, Si, S, Cl) and trace elements (<color=#3366CC>Ti, 80 ppm</color>, Mn, Cu, Fe) contents depend mostly on the soil and
the season.
<color=#3366CC>Carotenoids</color> can be found primarily in the leaves, where different forms of <color=#3366CC>lutein</color>, xanthophyll and carotene are present
(Table 2). Some carotenes are precursors of <color=#3366CC>vitamin A</color> (retinol), their retinol equivalents RE or retinol activity
equivalents per g dry weight are 1.33 for mature leaves and 0.9 for young leaves. Nettle contains much less carotenes
and retinol than carrots, which contain 8.35 RE per g fresh weight. Depending on the batch and the leaf and stem
content, nettle contains only traces of zeaxanthin or between 20–60 mg/kg of dry matter. Nettle contains ascorbic acid

(<color=#3366CC>vitamin C</color>), riboflavin (<color=#3366CC>vitamin B2</color>), <color=#3366CC>pantothenic acid</color>, vitamin K1 and tocopherols (<color=#3366CC>vitamin E</color>). The highest vitamin
contents can be found in the leaves.
Poultry: Egg yolk colouring in laying hens
In laying hens, nettle can be used as an egg yolk colourant instead of artificial pigments or other natural pigments
(derived from <color=#3366CC>marigold</color> for yellow). Nettle has high carotenoid contents, especially <color=#3366CC>lutein</color>, <color=#3366CC>-carotene</color> and zeaxanthin, of
which lutein and zeaxanthin act as yellow pigments. Feeding as little as 6.25 g dry nettle per kg feed is as effective as
the synthetic pigments to colour the egg yolk. Feeding nettle has no detrimental effect on the performance of the laying
hens or on the general quality of eggs.
Ruminants
Ruminants avoid fresh stinging nettles; however, if the nettles are wilted or dry, voluntary intake can be high.
Use in agriculture / horticulture

In the <color=#3366CC>European Union</color>, nettle extract can be used as an <color=#3366CC>insecticide</color>, <color=#3366CC>fungicide</color>, and <color=#3366CC>acaricide</color> under Basic Substance
regulations. As an insecticide, nettle extract can be used for the control of codling moth, diamondback moth, and spider
mites. As a fungicide, it can be used for the control of Pythium root rot, powdery mildew, early blight, <color=#3366CC>late blight</color>,
Septoria blight, Alternaria leaf spot, and grey mould.
Gardening
Nettles have a number of uses in the vegetable garden, including the potential for encouraging beneficial insects. Since
nettles prefer to grow in phosphorus-rich and nitrogen rich soils that have recently been disturbed (and thus aerated),
the growth of nettles is an indicator that an area has high fertility (especially <color=#3366CC>phosphate</color> and <color=#3366CC>nitrate</color>), and thus is an
<color=#3366CC>indicator</color> to gardeners as to the quality of the soil.
Nettles contain <color=#3366CC>nitrogenous</color> compounds, so are used as a <color=#3366CC>compost</color> activator or can be used to make a liquid fertiliser,
